When should a harbour close a lantern lane so that night traffic can recover? This essay answers that question for one named case, the Glasswater Harbour. The closure it treats in detail is the Lantern Lane, a marked channel closed to large night barges in the Glasswater light traffic. Fairness is used here as a judgement about purpose, evidence, and who bears the cost. It is not a slogan, and it is not filled in where a gathered file is silent. The brief allows the Glasswater Harbour, the Paper Bay, or the Ink Delta. The gathered files that can be read are about the Glasswater Harbour, so Paper Bay and the Ink Delta are not used as the case. Module code MOD4401ZZ is the practice module on that brief, and the short file title is MOD4401ZZ-1.

This essay asks when a made-up harbour should close a lantern lane. The case is the Glasswater Harbour. No mark scheme is attached. The answer uses only reasons that the opened notes give, and a reason they do not discuss stays outside it. Several notes could be kept only as abstracts, because the official address did not return a real file. One workshop note was opened in full. A claim that rests on an abstract does not go past that abstract, and a figure the note only cites from another work is not treated as a measurement this essay made.

An interest, here, is a reason a gathered note gives for caring how the night lane is shared. The notes do not share one definition and they do not rank the reasons. Pell, Quinn and Ash (2006) frame a balance between barge traffic and the lantern watch. Keel, Binder, Lumen and Marlow (2014) describe costs and benefits for the channel, the night crews, and the harbour desk. compares the lantern plan with a paper-bay scenario. Alden, Hopper and Quay (2024),, and North, South and Tide (2020) write from the crane shed and the buoy store. argue that conflicts of interest across the watch are part of the harbour's own rule. Counting an interest means one of these notes gives it as a reason. It does not mean a fair share or a winner has been found.

The lane itself is the first reason the modelling abstracts give. Pell, Quinn and Ash (2006) describe a closed channel. Night barges that leave the Paper Wharf pass the Ink Buoy, enter the Glasswater Harbour, and are eventually counted at the crane. They give the lane an approximate length of about 30 marked buoys and call it the harbour's largest night route under the 1971 lantern notice. They say the marked buoys sustain a steady watch, a visible channel, and a first-class night desk, and that the lane depends on a seasonal tide together with a variable fog. Annual shifts in the tide become long stretches of a dim channel. On that description, the lane is not a store of spare water. It is the place where the night traffic is counted. A closure upstream is therefore already a closure of the passage the harbour would otherwise keep open.

The same abstract says that extra barges and a new shed in the upstream basins are expected to reduce or redistribute the nights available to the lane. To study upstream and local changes, the authors built a coupled tide and lantern model on a one-buoy grid. Watch logs are sparse, so the model was compared with lantern charts rather than with point logs. The abstract says the scenario results can help the harbour desk balance the watch and the barge demand. The scenario magnitudes are not in the abstract, so they are not used. What the abstract does establish is a pair of interests: the watch, seen as a lit channel, and the barge demand, including upstream sheds. Both are reasons a decision has to weigh. Neither is given a number here.

Keel, Binder, Lumen and Marlow (2014) place that weighing across basins. Their abstract says the lane runs through Paper Bay, Ink Delta, and Glasswater Harbour, is in near-ordinary condition, and supports a marked channel and a night watch, while the basin crews are few and a new shed is inevitable. The three desks completed a shared diagnostic in 2010, funded by the three basins and the Glasswater desk. A central feature was a lane-wide passage assessment using a made-up tally the desks called the night count. The abstract says the scenarios of increasing barge use spelled out costs and benefits for the channel, for the night crews, and for the local and harbour desks, and that those results helped create a plan the desks were beginning to act on. Only the abstract was opened, so the findings are not reported here as figures. The interests the assessment was built to count are still clear: the channel, the crews tied to it, and the desks at local and harbour scale. A new shed is called inevitable. It is not treated as the only interest. The hope that the lane could illustrate three aims of a quiet harbour is a stated aim, not a result this essay can check.

adds a second pressure that the first note left out. The workshop abstract models lanterns and barge counts for 2050-2080 and 2070-2100 under a made-up fog scenario and five paper models, and it compares those runs with a local shed scenario. Past tide, fog, and watch hours were modified and passed through a lantern model. The simulations predict dimmer nights, with deeper gaps between buoys and less frequent clear passages. Fog is expected to matter more, in these runs, than a new shed. Extra lanterns along the lane are said to increase the lit hours and so to mitigate the local fog. Buoy types had distinct preferred gaps, brighter types are expected to lose count, and the variety of lanterns is expected to decline because many bright types are not widely hung. A closing acknowledgement thanks a supervisor. It is not a finding and it does not add an author. For the question of whose watch counts, the abstract treats a lit gap and a clear passage as conditions that can be lost, and it warns that a local shed plan is not the only change the lane faces. It does not give any user a present-day share of the night.

reports the same lane from the night watch at the northern buoy. Barge counting and lantern keeping remain the main work for most crews, while a paper market creates a need for a cash tally. The abstract draws on the Glasswater night-watch baseline and says the strategies at that buoy are highly varied, with risk tied to reliance on the lanterns. Other notes named as background were not opened and are not sources here. The abstract supports a crew interest in barges, lanterns, and cash, in a place exposed because it depends on the lane. It does not say how many nights that buoy uses, or who should give way if the lane is closed.

Read together, the opened notes support a bounded answer. An interest counts when one of these notes treats it as a reason for how the lantern lane is shared. The watch interest counts because the 2006 modelling abstract defines the decision as a balance with lantern demand, because Keel, Binder, Lumen and Marlow (2014) built scenarios around the channel, and because ties a bright buoy to a clear gap. Upstream sheds count because that modelling abstract expects extra barges to change the night count, and because the passage abstract sets a new shed beside local and harbour desks. Crews count because Alden, Hopper and Quay (2024) find the night market and the barge tally driving the take-up, with uneven benefits, and because finds barge counting and lantern keeping still carrying the northern buoy while cash needs grow. The shed desk counts because North, South and Tide (2020) show collection, cash, distance, and affordability already structuring access. The unlit gap and the night crews count because treat a purely barge claim on an infinite lane as a bad rule.

What does not follow is a winner. No opened note states a rule that would let one interest cancel the others. The modelling and passage papers, read only as abstracts, do not yield scenario tables. The watch abstracts do not yield a volume or a legal entitlement. The workshop note does not measure a release. Dimming in the fog runs may outweigh a new shed in those runs, but the abstract does not say local crews therefore lose their claim. Uneven benefits in Alden, Hopper and Quay (2024) show that naming an interest is not the same as sharing the benefit. Cash and distance in North, South and Tide (2020) show that an interest can count at harbour scale and still fail inside one shed. These interests count. The opened evidence does not authorise one ranked closure, and the gap is not filled by a share or a finding the notes do not give.

The Glasswater note again records a lantern, a barge, and a watch desk, and it still refuses a ranked winner.
